partes.p: Let's assume we have an open economy with demand for domestic goods:

where the real exchange rate $\varepsilon$ , investment $I$, government spending $G$, and taxes $T$ are assumed to be exogenous. The consumption is given by
where $c_{0}>$ 0 and $c_{1}\in (0, 1)$. Demand for imports and demand for exports are given, respectively, by
$$\text{IM }= c_{2}\cdot Y \cdot \varepsilon$$
$$X = Y^{*} - \alpha \cdot \varepsilon$$
where $\alpha > 0, c_{2}\in (0, c_{1})$. Finally, the good market equilbirium is characterized by the condition $Y = Z$.

[10 Points] Draw the graph of domestic demand for goods, and the demand for domestic goods, as a function of income on the same chart. When you draw the graph, assume that $Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon > 0$. Do both demands have the same slope? If not, which one is fatter, and why? Using an additional chart underneath the one you just drew, draw net exports as a function of income and specify at which point trade balance arises.

solucao.p: [10 Points] Draw the graph of domestic demand for goods, and the demand for domestic goods, as a function of income on the same chart. When you draw the graph, assume that $Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon > 0$. Do both demands have the same slope? If not, which one is fatter, and why? Using an additional chart underneath the one you just drew, draw net exports as a function of income and specify at which point trade balance arises.

The demand for domestic goods (ZZ) is fatter than the domestic demand for goods (DD). Indeed, when the income of a country increases, only a fraction of the increase in demand goes to domestic goods, and part of the increase of demand is absorbed by foreign goods. The trade balance is the difference between the demand for domestic goods and the domestic demand for goods.

partes.p: [15 Points] Compute GDP and trade balance as a function of exogenous variables and parameters.

solucao.p: [15 Points] Compute GDP and trade balance as a function of exogenous variables and parameters.
At the equilibrium, output must be equal to demand for domestic goods, so that we have
$$Y = C + I + G + X - \frac{IM}{\varepsilon}$$
$$\Leftarrow \Rightarrow Y = c_{0}+ c_{1}(Y - T) + I + G + Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon - c_{2}Y$$
$$\Leftarrow \Rightarrow (1 - c_{1}+ c_{2})Y = c_{0}- c_{1}T + I + G + Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon$$
$$\Leftarrow \Rightarrow Y = \frac{c_{0}- c_{1}T + I + G + Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon}{1 - c_{1}+ c_{2}}$$
From that, we conclude that trade balance is given by:
NX $= X -$ IM$/\varepsilon$
$$= Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon - c_{2}Y$$
$$= Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon - c_{2}\frac{c_{0}- c_{1}T + I + G + Y^{*} - \alpha \varepsilon}{1 - c_{1}+ c_{2}}$$

In this case, the government should depreciate the real exchange rate by $1/\alpha$ to balance the effect on trade defcit. Such an effect would have no effect on GDP, unlike the previous policy. Therefore, exchange rate depreciation is more efficient to maintain the trade balance.
